title: Vijayanagara Empire
wiki_lead:
The Vijayanagara Empire, also known as the Karnāta Empire, was a late medieval Hindu empire that ruled much of Southern India. It was established in 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty.
The empire rose to prominence following the disruption caused by the Delhi Sultanate incursions into the Deccan during the early 14th century. At its territorial peak under Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529), it held primacy across the peninsula, pushing the  Deccan sultanates north of the Tungabhadra–Krishna doab and annexing coastal Gajapati territories up to the Krishna River. At its greatest extent, its domain encompassed moddern Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Goa, southern Kerala and some parts of Telangana and southern Maharashtra.
The empire survived until 1646, though its central authority diminished sharply following its defeat by allied Deccan Sultanates at the Battle of Talikota in 1565. The empire took its name from the capital city of Vijayanagara (near modern Hampi), whose extensive ruins are designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Chronicles by foreign visitors—including Domingo Paes, Fernão Nunes, Niccolò de' Conti, and Abdur Razzak—along with indigenous epigraphy and archeological excavations, form the primary documentary record of the empire.
Its architectural legacy is visible across India, characterized by a synthesis of earlier Chalukya, Hoysala, Pandya, and Chola forms in monumental temple complexes. They feature tall gateway towers (rajagopurams), and pillared halls (mandapas). State-sponsored irrigation canals and reservoirs supported intense agriculture and urban growth. Court patronage also stimulated literary production in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, and Sanskrit with topics such as astronomy, mathematics, medicine, fiction, musicology, historiography and theater gaining popularity. Carnatic music developed into its classical structural framework during this era.

Name
'Vijayanagara' translates as 'City of Victory'. Contemporary inscriptions and literature frequently referred to the kingdom as 'Karnata Rajya' ('Karnata Kingdom'),  as seen in Krishnadevaraya's Sanskrit drama Jambavati Kalyanam and Ramarajabhushana's Telugu work Vasu Charitamu. Early Portuguese and European chroniclers commonly designated the realm the "The Kingdom of Narsinga", an epithet derived from the Saluva ruler Narasimha Deva Raya or Narasimha Raya II.


History


Background and origin theories

Prior to the raise of Vijayanagara, the major Hindu kingdoms of the Deccan and peninsular India—the Seunas (Yadava Empire) of Devagiri, the Kakatiya dynasty of Warangal, the Pandyan Empire of Madurai, and the Hoysalas of Belur—were subjected to repeated raids and territorial annexations by the Delhi Sultanate during the reigns of Alauddin Khalji (his general Malik Kafur) and Muhammad bin Tughluq. In the Tungabhadra basin, local commanders established the short-lived Kampili kingdom in the 1320s, which fell to Tughluq forces around 1327–1328 after its defenders performed jauhar (ritual self-immolation). The administrative and military vacuum created by the collapse of these regional polities provided the context for the establishment of Vijayanagara Kingdom in 1336.
Historians debate the regional and linguistic origins of the founders, Harihara I and Bukka I. One view posits that they were Kannada-speaking officers in the service of the Hoysala Empire stationed on its northern frontier—to defend against Muslim invasions—along the Tungabhadra. Alternative thesis holds that they were Telugu commanders initially serving the Kakatiyas of Warangal, who were captured during the Tughluq conquest. Later literary tradition credits the Advaita sage Vidyaranya of the Sringeri Sharada Peetham with inspiring their return to Hinduism and guiding the founding of the capital. Contemporary inscriptional evidence for Vidyaranya's direct involvement in 1336 remains limited.

grok_lead: The Vijayanagara Empire was a Hindu empire in southern India founded in 1336 CE by brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty, who served in the administrations of the Kakatiya and Kampili kingdoms, consolidated power by annexing Hoysala territories by 1346, and, guided by the sage Vidyaranya as their spiritual advisorâwho is traditionally credited with authoring the Sarva-Darsana-Sangraha, a compendium surveying sixteen Indian philosophical systems from an Advaita Vedanta perspective, and fostered temple construction and Vedic scholarshipâestablished it amid the collapse of regional powers like the Hoysalas and Kakatiyas under pressure from the Delhi Sultanate's incursions, positioning the empire as a defender of Hindu dharma. With its capital at Vijayanagaraâmodern Hampi in Karnatakaâthe empire functioned as a bulwark against northern Muslim expansions, sustaining Hindu political and cultural dominance for over three centuries until its effective dissolution around 1646 CE. Spanning dynasties including Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, and Aravidu, it governed vast territories from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal, fostering economic vitality through trade in spices, textiles, and diamonds, alongside sophisticated irrigation systems that supported agriculture. The empire's zenith occurred under Tuluva Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509â1529), whose conquests subdued the Gajapatis of Odisha and Bahmanis of the Deccan, while his court patronized literature in Kannada, Telugu, and Sanskrit, exemplified by poets like Allasani Peddana and temple endowments. Architectural legacies, characterized by towering gopurams, intricate mandapas, and fortified complexes at Hampi, blended Dravidian styles with Indo-Islamic influences, as seen in structures like the Vitthala Temple's stone chariot and the elephant stables. Military defeats, notably the 1565 Battle of Talikota against a Deccan Sultanate alliance, precipitated the capital's devastation and administrative fragmentation, though successor Nayaka states perpetuated regional influence into the 18th century.
